lessons.title: Debt, Equity and Net Worth: How a Company Is Funded

children.text: Two snack factories sit on the same industrial estate outside Indore. Same machines, same products, same ₹6 crore of operating profit. One was built with the owners' money. The other was built with a bank term loan. In a good year the borrower earns a better return for its owners. In a bad year it is the one that gets a call from the bank.

That difference is capital structure: the mix of borrowed money and owners' money funding the business. It does not change how good your product is, and it changes almost everything about how much risk the company can carry.

body.text: Debt magnifies whatever the business does. Good years get better, bad years get dangerous, and the operations themselves do not change at all.

children.text: The Two Sources of Money
The right side of the balance sheet has only two kinds of funding, and they behave in opposite ways.

columns.label: Debt
points: Interest must be paid whatever the year looks like
Lenders rank ahead of owners if things go wrong
Interest is tax deductible, which lowers the real cost
No ownership given away, but covenants restrict your choices

columns.label: Equity
points: Dividends are optional and can be skipped
No repayment date, the money is permanent
Owners are paid last, after every creditor
Dividends are paid out of post-tax profit, so no tax shield
Ownership is diluted and new shareholders get a say

children.text: Indian companies draw on a familiar menu within those two buckets.

body.caption: Where the funding actually comes from

cells: The base of almost every Indian business, built up year after year
Private equity or venture capital, IPO, QIP, rights issue
Growth capital, expansion, or an exit route for early investors
Plant, machinery, buildings, repaid over several years
Working capital, repayable on demand, drawn and repaid continuously
Larger companies raising from the bond and money markets
Rented offices, warehouses and vehicles, on the balance sheet under Ind AS 116
Startup funding rounds, debt-like until they convert into equity

body.label: Why debt looks cheap
body.context: Interest is deductible before tax is computed, so at a 26% effective tax rate a 9.5% loan costs the company about 7.0% net. Equity carries no such shield. This tax advantage is the honest half of the case for debt. The dishonest half is pretending the repayment obligation is not real.

children.text: The Four Numbers Lenders and Boards Watch
Take the Kesari Foods balance sheet from Lesson 3.1: net worth ₹21 crore, term loan ₹10 crore, cash credit ₹3 crore, cash ₹1.5 crore, operating profit ₹6 crore and finance costs ₹1.5 crore.

stats.label: Debt to equity
stats.context: ₹13 crore of borrowings against ₹21 crore of net worth

body.caption: How many times over the year's profit covers the year's interest

children.text: Interest coverage is the number to watch if you only watch one. Above about 4 times, interest is a manageable line item. Below 2, a single bad quarter starts to threaten the company's ability to service its loans, and lenders begin to take an interest in decisions you thought were yours.

body.title: Can this company carry its debt?
body.prompt: A Surat textile firm reports operating profit of ₹18 crore and finance costs of ₹7.5 crore for the year. What is its interest coverage, in times?
body.explanation: ₹18 crore ÷ ₹7.5 crore = 2.4 times. Each year the business earns only 2.4 times its interest bill, so a 30% fall in operating profit would leave very little headroom. Lenders typically want comfortable coverage and often write a minimum into the loan agreement.

body.title: Debt, net of what?
body.textWithBlank: Total borrowings minus cash and cash equivalents is called ___ debt.
body.explanation: Net debt recognises that a company holding large cash balances is less indebted than its gross borrowings suggest. A company with more cash than debt is said to be net cash, which is the position Infosys and several large Indian IT firms hold.

children.text: What Leverage Actually Does to Returns

Here are the two identical factories, both earning an operating profit of ₹6 crore on total funding of ₹34 crore. The first is funded entirely by owners. The second uses ₹13 crore of debt at about 11.5%, giving interest of ₹1.5 crore. Tax is 26% in both cases.

body.caption: Same business, two funding structures (₹ crore)

children.text: The borrower earns less profit and a better return, because the same profit is spread over less owners' money. Now run a bad year in which operating profit falls from ₹6 crore to ₹2 crore, something a single lost customer or a monsoon-hit season can do.

body.title: Return on equity in a good year and a bad year

children.text: In the bad year the all-equity factory still earns 4.4% for its owners. The borrower earns 1.8%, because ₹1.5 crore of interest is paid before the owners see anything. Push operating profit below ₹1.5 crore and the borrower makes a loss while the other is still profitable. Nothing about the product, the market or the team differs. Only the funding does.

body.text: Leverage is a multiplier, not a strategy. It is defensible when cash flows are predictable, such as a long-term contract or a utility, and dangerous when they are cyclical, such as commodities, construction or discretionary consumer goods. The Indian corporate distress of the last decade, from infrastructure to telecom, was almost always leverage meeting a downturn.

body.title: Where does leverage bite?
body.question: Two companies have identical operations and identical EBITDA. One has debt to equity of 0.3, the other 2.0. A recession cuts EBITDA by 40% at both. What is the most likely difference in outcome?
options: Both report the same percentage fall in net profit
The leveraged company reports a much larger percentage fall in net profit and may breach its loan covenants
The leveraged company is unaffected because interest is fixed
The low-debt company suffers more because it has no tax shield
body.explanation: Interest does not fall with EBITDA. The leveraged company pays the same interest out of a much smaller operating profit, so its net profit falls far more sharply in percentage terms, and coverage ratios can fall through the minimums written into its loan agreements.

children.text: Covenants: The Strings Attached
Loan agreements carry covenants, promises the company makes to the lender about how it will behave. Managers meet them the day a plan is blocked for a reason that has nothing to do with the plan.
Financial covenants:
a ceiling on debt to equity, a floor on interest coverage or debt service coverage, sometimes a minimum net worth. Tested quarterly or annually.
Negative covenants:
no further borrowing, no sale of key assets, no dividend above a level, no change in control, all without the lender's consent.
Information covenants:
monthly or quarterly statements, stock and receivable statements for working capital limits, audited accounts within a fixed period.

A breach rarely means the loan is instantly recalled. It usually means a waiver request, a higher interest rate, tighter conditions or fresh security. That is why a capital expenditure proposal, a large dividend or an acquisition goes past treasury before it goes to the board.

body.title: Reading the borrowings note in an annual report

children.text: The face of the balance sheet gives one number. The note behind it tells you whether the company is comfortable or cornered.
Secured or unsecured:
what has been pledged. A charge over the plant, or over inventory and receivables, limits what can be sold or refinanced later.
Fixed or floating rate:
floating rate loans reprice when the RBI moves the repo rate, so a rate cycle changes the interest bill without anything else changing.
Repayment schedule:
how much falls due in the next twelve months. A company with modest total debt but a large repayment next year has a refinancing problem, not a leverage problem.
Covenants and defaults:
any breach during the year must be disclosed, along with whether a waiver was obtained.
Credit rating:
agencies such as CRISIL, ICRA and CARE Ratings rate borrowers, and a downgrade raises the cost of every future rupee borrowed.

body.label: CRISIL Ratings
body.description: Search an Indian company to see its credit rating and rating rationale. The rationale is a free, unusually candid read on a company's leverage, cash flows and refinancing risk.

children.text: What a Comfortable Balance Sheet Looks Like

Britannia Industries shows the conservative end of the spectrum. As at 31 March 2025 it reported borrowings of about ₹1,247 crore against net worth of about ₹4,356 crore, a debt to equity of roughly 0.29. Its FY25 operating profit after depreciation was about ₹2,863 crore against finance costs of ₹139 crore, which is interest coverage of around 20 times. This is a company for which interest is a rounding error, and it can fund a bad year, a new plant and a dividend without asking anyone's permission.

stats.label: Britannia debt to equity
stats.context: ₹1,247 crore of borrowings on ₹4,356 crore of net worth

stats.label: Britannia interest coverage
stats.context: Operating profit ₹2,863 crore against interest ₹139 crore

body.text: There is no universally correct level of debt. A power utility with 25-year contracted revenue can carry debt to equity of 2 or 3 comfortably. A fashion retailer at the same level would be fragile. Judge leverage against how predictable the cash flow is, never against a textbook number.

body.title: Fund the new line with debt or equity?
body.scenario: Kesari Foods wants to add a ₹12 crore production line. Net worth is ₹21 crore, existing borrowings are ₹13 crore, EBITDA is ₹8 crore and interest coverage is 4 times. The promoter can bring in ₹12 crore of fresh equity from a family trust, or the company can take a term loan at about 11%. The CFO asks for your recommendation as head of operations.
body.prompt: Lay out the trade-off with numbers, and say what you would need to know before deciding.
body.modelAnswer:
If funded by debt:
1. Borrowings rise to ₹25 crore and debt to equity moves from 0.62 to about 1.19, which many lenders treat as the outer edge of comfort for a mid-sized manufacturer.
2. Interest rises by roughly ₹1.32 crore a year at 11%, so total interest goes to about ₹2.82 crore. Unless operating profit rises, coverage falls from 4.0 to about 2.1 times, close to the level at which covenants bite.
3. Ownership is untouched and the tax shield lowers the effective cost to about 8% after tax.
If funded by equity:
4. Net worth rises to ₹33 crore and debt to equity falls to about 0.39, leaving room to borrow later for working capital as the new line fills up.
5. No fixed obligation, so a delayed ramp-up does not threaten anything.
6. The promoter's stake is diluted unless the family trust is already an existing shareholder, and the money comes with an expectation of returns even without a contractual one.
What I would need to know before deciding:
7. The ramp-up profile: how long until the line runs at a volume that pays for itself, and what the incremental EBITDA is once it does.
8. Existing covenants on the ₹10 crore term loan, particularly any ceiling on debt to equity or a floor on coverage.
9. Working capital impact: extra volume needs extra inventory and receivables, which needs its own funding, roughly ₹10 crore of working capital for every ₹50 crore of sales at current ratios.
10. The downside case: what coverage looks like if volumes come in 30% below plan for two years.
My recommendation: a mix, for example ₹7 crore of equity and ₹5 crore of debt, keeps debt to equity at about 0.64 and coverage close to 2.9 times while still capturing part of the tax shield.

body.title: Check your own company's funding
steps: Add all borrowings, long-term and short-term, from the latest balance sheet, and divide by net worth.
Subtract cash and equivalents to get net debt.
Compute interest coverage: operating profit divided by finance costs.
Open the borrowings note and find how much debt falls due within the next twelve months.
Check whether the loans are fixed or floating rate, and what a one percentage point rate move would cost.
If the company is rated, read the latest rating rationale from CRISIL, ICRA or CARE Ratings.

cards.definition: The mix of debt and equity funding a business.
Share capital plus reserves. What the owners have put in and left in.
Total borrowings divided by net worth. A measure of how leveraged a company is.
Total borrowings minus cash and cash equivalents.
Operating profit divided by finance costs. How many times over the year's profit covers the interest bill.
The use of borrowed money, which magnifies returns in both directions.
A promise to a lender about ratios, borrowings, asset sales or disclosure, which restricts what management can do.
The reduction in tax that results from interest being deductible, which lowers the effective cost of debt.

points: Every rupee on the asset side is funded by either debt or equity, and the two behave in opposite ways.
Debt is cheaper because interest is tax deductible, and riskier because it must be paid whatever the year brings.
Leverage raises returns in good years and destroys them in bad ones, without changing the underlying business.
Interest coverage is the single most useful leverage number. Comfortable is roughly 4 times or better, and below 2 is fragile.
Covenants restrict borrowing, asset sales and dividends, so check them before proposing capital spending.
The right level of debt depends on how predictable the cash flows are, not on a textbook ratio.

body.text: Kesari Foods and the Surat textile firm are fictional, and the interest rates and tax rate used are illustrative. Britannia figures are FY25 consolidated numbers derived from screener.in. Nothing here is investment advice or a recommendation on how to fund a specific business.
